# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. A gallon of it weighs about 8.3 pounds, and a column of water just one inch square but a foot tall exerts nearly half a pound of pressure per square inch at its base. This simple fact—water pressure comes from weight and elevation—explains almost everything about how a city water system works, and why getting water to the fifteenth floor of an apartment building is a genuinely interesting engineering problem.

## The Fundamental Principle: Elevation as Energy

Water in a municipal system is pushed by two things: pumps and gravity. Engineers often talk in terms of "head," which is simply the height of a water column, expressed in feet or meters. Every foot of elevation gives water about 0.43 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. A reservoir sitting on a hill 200 feet above a neighborhood provides roughly 86 psi at the taps below—no moving parts required, just physics.
